comments.author: @jvangeene
comments.text:
So exciting again to hear about this AI Research development, and well covered - thanks Wes! To me this is a logical, more or less anticipated, next step. Since the the first "accepted peer reviewed paper" was in the field of ML (submitted at a ML conference) it makes sense to continue on that path and then try to replicate other paper, thus trying to improve AI research agents. I would expect soon - depending on how much GPU power is dedicated to it - AI researchers WILL outperform PhD level human researchers in this field, simply because models are already improving (mind you - they used Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and NOT 3.7 or Gemini 2.5 Ultra with 1m context window). But more importantly because the replication process itself will create better AI Researchers since they will use it (I assume) to self-improve the 'open source scaffolding' (I guess the finetuning and agentic features) of the AI Agents. So every iteration in this AI replication process will give the opportunity to keep learning and improving the AI Agents capability, while a humen PhD level AI scientist will plateau much sooner...
So - my bet will be that within a very limited number of iterations (e.g. 1 million small improvements) an AI ML research Agent will have reached that 'magical' point where it will soon sky-rocket into the sublime. Since I am not well versed into the AI science domain, I cannot predict the exact number of iterations. But I think an AI can predict this, based on the progress so far and the potential for improvements in every iteration.
My next question would be - what are the next science domains that are well-suited for AI research replication? Which sciences can be  executed relatively autonomous? Since that is basically what ML makes such a great playground for AI research. Biochemics for instance could be interesting, but mind you - most science still IS BASED IN THE PHYSICAL WORLD and thus relies on some human interaction (at least for now).
Interesting times.
